items.title: The direction of a cross product is a convention — and the universe doesn't care
items.claim: The cross product a x b gives a vector perpendicular to both. But why does it point UP rather than DOWN? The right-hand rule is a convention. A left-handed convention would also work — and the laws of physics don't depend on which we pick.

options.text: A physical fact about the universe
The cross product is a pseudovector (axial vector): its components reverse sign under coordinate reflection. The 'direction' it points is defined by our choice of orientation convention
Only a useful guide for memorisation

items.reveal:
A 'true' (polar) vector points in a definite physical direction. Velocity, force, displacement are vectors. Under a mirror reflection, the components perpendicular to the mirror reverse; components along it don't.

A pseudovector (axial vector) — like angular velocity, magnetic field, torque, cross product results — behaves differently under reflection: components ALONG the mirror reverse, perpendicular ones don't.

Intuition: angular velocity is 'how fast you're spinning, and which way the axis points'. The direction along the axis is a convention (right-hand rule). In a mirror, a top spinning clockwise looks anticlockwise — its angular velocity 'vector' reverses, even though no physical change happened.

Maxwell's equations: electric field is a polar vector; magnetic field is an axial vector. Lorentz force F = qE + qv x B mixes the two correctly because v x B (vector cross pseudovector) yields a polar vector.

Physical predictions don't depend on convention. Computed cross products in left-handed and right-handed coordinate systems give opposite vectors — but the OBSERVABLE outcomes are identical.

This has been a source of confusion for centuries. The modern formulation uses differential forms or geometric algebra to avoid pseudovectors and make orientation explicit.
items.why: Vectors feel like they should have definite physical directions. Cross products produce 'directions' that depend on arbitrary convention — and physics has to be carefully formulated so observable predictions don't.

items.title: Just 23 people give a 50/50 chance of a shared birthday
items.claim: How many people do you need in a room for it to be more likely than not that two share a birthday? Most people guess 100 or 180. The answer is 23.
items.prompt: Why is the threshold so low?

options.text: With 23 people there are 23 choose 2 = 253 possible pairs, each with about a 1/365 chance of matching; the question is not 'matches me' but 'any match anywhere', which has many more chances
Coincidences happen because of cosmic alignment

items.reveal:
The probability that NO two people in a group of n share a birthday is (365/365)(364/365)(363/365)...((365-n+1)/365).

For n = 23, this product equals about 0.493. Probability of AT LEAST ONE match equals 1 - 0.493 = 0.507. Just over 50 percent.
For n = 41, probability of a match is about 90 percent.
For n = 70, about 99.9 percent.

Intuition fails because we ask 'does someone share MY birthday?' — that requires n ≈ 253 for 50 percent. The real question allows ANY pair to match, and the number of pairs grows as n choose 2 ≈ n squared / 2.

This 'birthday attack' is important in cryptography: collision resistance of a hash function with N possible outputs only protects against attackers who try fewer than about square root of N inputs. A 128-bit hash gives only 64-bit collision security.
items.why: Counting pairs is qualitatively different from counting people. Pair counts grow quadratically, so coincidences are far more likely than a head-count suggests.

items.title: A coin doesn't 'owe' you a head after 10 tails — but a casino does
items.claim: 10 tails in a row. Probability of the next flip being heads is still 1/2. The coin has no memory. Casinos exploit the gambler's fallacy — players betting against 'streaks' actually have no edge.
items.prompt: Why doesn't the law of large numbers help short-term?

options.text: The law of large numbers only applies to dice

LLN guarantees long-run frequency convergence to expected probability, but does NOT mean short-term deviations must be 'corrected' by reverse outcomes. Each flip is independent: past results carry no information
Tails must come back to balance heads

items.reveal_title: Gambler's fallacy and the law of large numbers (correctly stated)
items.reveal:
Gambler's fallacy: the false belief that, in a sequence of independent random events, recent 'streaks' make the opposite outcome more likely.

Monte Carlo Casino, 1913: black came up 26 times in a row at a roulette table. Players reportedly lost millions betting on red, believing the streak 'must' end. Each spin was independent; the probability of red on the 27th spin was the same as on the first (~18/37 for a European wheel, less than 1/2 because of the green zero).

LLN says: as n increases, the SAMPLE PROPORTION approaches the TRUE PROBABILITY. After 10 tails in a row out of 10 flips, the proportion is 100% tails. After a million more fair flips (with roughly 500,000 each side), the cumulative proportion approaches 50%. But this happens by SWAMPING the early streak, not by REVERSING it. The next flip after 10 tails is still 50/50.

Inverse mistake (hot-hand fallacy): assuming streaks WILL continue (sports). Actually mixed evidence — some sports skills appear to genuinely streak (basketball shooting under some studies), others don't. Distinguishing real streaks from spurious ones requires careful statistics.

Gambler's fallacy explains casino profits even when individual games are 'fair-ish'. House edges (~5% in roulette) compound over many bets; players betting against streaks don't gain anything.

The broader cognitive pattern: humans expect randomness to be uniform. Real randomness has clusters and streaks. Mistaking real randomness for 'patterns' is one of the most consistently studied errors in cognitive psychology.
items.why: Past results feel like they should influence future probabilities. They don't, for independent events. Misunderstanding this drives gambling losses, conspiracy theories, and bad predictions across domains.
